summary:
MARSBOUND is an interactive browser-based game designed for children aged 7–12, developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge's "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge.

Players take the role of Commander of a Mars outpost and guide their crew through three Martian days (Sols), facing five challenges involving life support, radiation protection, power management, greenhouse farming, and communication delays with Earth. Every decision involves trade-offs that affect limited resources, including oxygen, water, power, and crew health.

The game incorporates real NASA data, including historical solar flare records from NASA's DONKI database and scientific findings about Mars radiation and space exploration. It clearly distinguishes verified NASA information from simplified game mechanics. Players experience the consequences of their decisions through delayed effects, a solar storm event, and four possible mission endings.

Through interactive gameplay, NASA-based educational content, and a final Mission Debrief, MARSBOUND makes the challenges of human exploration of Mars more engaging and accessible while encouraging critical thinking, resource management, and informed decision-making.
details:
About MARSBOUND

MARSBOUND is an interactive educational browser game that puts players in the role of a Junior Astronaut Commander responsible for managing a Mars outpost and keeping its crew alive for three Martian days (Sols).

How It Works

Players face five mission challenges:

  • Life Support: Manage oxygen and water supplies.
  • Radiation Protection: Make decisions to protect the crew from radiation.
  • Power Management: Keep the outpost powered.
  • Greenhouse Farming: Manage food production and delayed harvests.
  • Communication with Earth: Experience the delays involved in communicating across the distance between Earth and Mars.

Players can choose the order in which they tackle challenges. Each challenge presents three possible decisions, with different resource costs and consequences.

The game tracks four resources: Oxygen, Water, Power, and Crew Health. Decisions affect these resources, and some consequences are delayed. A solar storm occurs at the end of Sol 2 if the crew has not been adequately sheltered. The mission concludes with one of four possible endings, followed by a Mission Debrief explaining the outcome and what players could improve.

NASA Data and Educational Value

MARSBOUND incorporates real NASA resources and scientific information. It uses historical solar flare records from NASA's DONKI database to determine the solar storm scenario. It also introduces real space-exploration concepts, including the International Space Station's water recovery system, Mars radiation measurements, NASA's research into fission power, the Veggie plant-growth experiment, and Earth–Mars communication delays.

Each challenge includes a "How NASA handles this" section that connects the gameplay to real space exploration. The game clearly distinguishes verified NASA information from simplified numbers and mechanics created for gameplay balance. It is an educational simulation, not a prediction of an actual Mars mission. NASA has not yet landed humans on Mars.

Creativity and Impact

Instead of simply presenting facts about space, MARSBOUND lets children learn through decisions and consequences. Players experience the difficult trade-offs involved in managing a crew and a remote outpost, making concepts such as resource conservation, radiation protection, and delayed communication easier to understand.

The intended impact is to make space exploration more engaging for children while encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, planning, and scientific curiosity.

Technology Used

  • React 19 and JSX
  • Vite 8
  • JavaScript
  • Plain CSS
  • HTML Canvas for custom scenes and icons
  • Vitest for testing
  • ESLint for code quality

The game logic is organized into reusable JavaScript functions, separate from the React interface. The game uses local assets and does not require user accounts or a backend. Player nicknames remain in memory, and the game can operate offline.

Use of AI Tools

AI tools, including ChatGPT, Claude Code, and Gemini, were used as development assistance during the project. They helped with coding, debugging, refining written content, and documentation. The team directed the project concept, made the design and development decisions, tested the implementation, and reviewed the final work. AI assistance was used as a supporting tool rather than a replacement for the team's own work.
